literal: 'Later we will know' without saying, may you do virtue; indeed that [is at] perishing time [an] undying companion.
translation: Do not delay doing good by saying 'We will see to it later.' When the time comes for you to die, virtue will be your only undying companion.
modern: 'பிறகு பார்த்துக்கொள்ளலாம்' என்று காலம் கடத்தாமல் இப்போதே அறத்தைச் செய்யுங்கள். ஒருவருடைய உயிர் பிரியும் காலத்தில் அவருக்கு அழியாத துணையாக இருப்பது அந்த அறம் மட்டுமே.
explanation: This couplet warns against the common human tendency to postpone doing good. The phrase 'aṉṟu aṟivām' captures the excuse of putting off virtue until later in life. The poet urges the reader to practice virtue immediately without making such excuses. The striking contrast between 'poṉṟum kāl' (the time of perishing) and 'poṉṟā tuṇai' (an imperishable companion) highlights that when the body dies, only one's accumulated virtue remains as an eternal support.
